activities.caption: file each point defect by its role
activities.name: msPointBuckets

config.prompt: The point-defect census — file each resident:

items.label: the missing atom every crystal has, in thermal equilibrium
an extra atom jammed between lattice sites — rare, hugely strained
a foreign atom on a lattice site — zinc in copper
a small atom in a gap — carbon in iron
for copper near melting, roughly one lattice site in 10⁵ is empty

config.why: All solid-state diffusion is vacancy traffic; all solid-solution strengthening is solute atoms obstructing dislocations.

activities.anchor: Take the defects out of a metal and you get a different problem
activities.caption: find the line the mechanism refutes
activities.name: msPerfectSpot

config.prompt: One line of this design note is wrong — click it:
lines: With no dislocations able to move, a metal cannot yield.
It stays elastic until it snaps in brittle fashion at enormous stress.
So the best possible metal would contain zero defects of any kind.
Defects give metals their forgiving failure mode.
Strength engineering manages which defects move, where, and when.
config.correction: A defect-free crystal would be the disaster, not the ideal — plasticity IS dislocation motion, and without it there is no warning before fracture.
config.why: Defects are not blemishes but the working parts of materials.

activities.anchor: like shuffling a carpet across a floor by pushing a ruck along it
activities.caption: pair each strengthening recipe with its dislocation fence
activities.name: msFenceMatch

config.prompt: Anything that obstructs dislocation motion strengthens the metal — pair recipe with fence:

pairs.right: solute atoms blocking the glide plane
grain boundaries — halve the grain size, strength rises with the inverse square root
interstitial carbon jammed into the lattice

config.why: Metallurgy's strength menu is a list of dislocation fences — the real stress to move a dislocation is typically a thousand times less than the perfect-lattice calculation.

activities.anchor: announces itself: the part yields, necks
activities.caption: walk the warning question
activities.name: msWarningBranch

config.root: The design question is never only "how strong?" — it is "how much warning?".

start.text: You are specifying a pressure vessel. What failure philosophy do you demand of the material?

choices.label: Fail-soft — yield, neck, absorb energy by plastic flow before separating
Fail-sudden — maximum strength regardless of mode

soft.text: Ductile failure announces itself: the plastic zone at a crack tip blunts the tip and consumes energy — which is why pressure vessels, bridges and aircraft are specified ductile.

choices.label: Now the window question: why ceramics are not structural
choices.feedback: The brittle side of the hinge.

sudden.text: Brittle failure gives no warning — crack propagation at acoustic speeds, at or below full design load, with almost no energy absorbed. The vessel spec moves to a ductile alloy.

choices.label: Continue to the window question
choices.feedback: The brittle side of the hinge.

ceramic.text: A brittle ceramic's immobile dislocations leave the crack tip sharp — nothing but bond-breaking resists the crack, which is why windows are not structural.

config.why: The difference is structural, not mystical: mobile dislocations blunt; locked-in dislocations leave the tip sharp.

activities.anchor: Every flaw is a magnifying glass
activities.caption: call the stress at the tip
activities.name: msGriffithEstimate

config.prompt: A 1-micron scratch with an atomically sharp tip sits under a nominal 100 MPa. Roughly what local stress does the tip concentrate?
config.why: σ_local ≈ 2σ·√(a/ρ) ≈ 14,000 MPa — well above the ~7 GPa needed to break silicate bonds, which is why glass is 100× weaker than its atoms demand.
config.context: Griffith's energy balance gives σ_c = √(2Eγ/πa) ≈ 116 MPa for that scratch — the largest flaw, not the bond strength, sets a brittle solid's strength.

activities.caption: the toughness league, upper bounds plotted
activities.name: msToughnessChart

activities.caption: rebuild the fatigue life, stage by stage
activities.name: msFatigueOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the fatigue sequence, cycle by cycle:
items: Nominally elastic loading still produces local plasticity at stress concentrators — fillets, rivet holes, inclusions
Reversed slip extrudes and intrudes microscopic persistent slip bands — the crack starters
The crack grows a little every cycle — Paris law, growth rate scaling with the stress-intensity range (m typically 2–4)
The critical size from fracture mechanics is reached
Final fracture: the surface shows beach marks — rings from each duty period — around a sudden fibrous snap zone
config.why: Fatigue accounts for the large majority of mechanical service failures — death by repetition, below yield strength.

config.text: Every cycle spends a share of life (Miner's rule), whether or not anything looks different — so the honest inference from "worked fine for a decade" is that %%0%%, not intuition, say what comes next.
config.hint: What converts accumulated damage into a schedule.
